newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU faces grain export subsidy cash squeeze.
newsitem.headline: EU faces grain export subsidy cash squeeze.

text.p: The European Union, anxious to avoid another grain export subsidy war as bumper crops force world prices down, said on Wednesday that budgetary curbs would force it to take a cautious approach to subsidies.
World wheat prices have halved since April when stocks seemed to be in danger of running out after drought devastated crops across the globe.
A record EU grain harvest and massive crops by other major producers, such as Argentina and Australia, have sent prices into a sharp downwards spiral.

In order to remain competitive on world markets, the EU restored wheat export subsidies in September after a break of nearly a year during which it taxed exports to prevent an exodus of grain attracted by higher international prices.
EU export subsidies have since risen sharply to around 22 Ecus ($28) a tonne, raising the hackles of the United States, its main competitor.
The EU's executive Commission said it was merely tracking the downward trend in world prices using the U.S. soft red winter wheat as a benchmark.

"We have taken care to always follow, rather than to lead, world prices - in particular U.S. prices...," David Roberts, the Commission deputy director general for agriculture, told a grains conference.
The EU would be forced to be extremely cautious about further increases in export subsidies during the rest of the 1996/97 (July-June) season because of budgetary problems, he said.
The conference was organised by Agra Europe, a consultancy which publishes newsletters on EU affairs.

"In the immediate future our main difficulty is more likely to be with our budget resources than with our WTO (World Trade Organisation) commitments," said Roberts, who is in charge of international agricultural relations and the farm budget.
He noted that the current EU subsidy for wheat was about five times higher than the average level of 4.25 Ecus a tonne included in the draft 1997 budget.
"Therefore, we have every interest in seeing the refund fall rather than pursuing an aggressive subsidy policy involving an increase in refunds," he said.

The EU easily met its WTO commitments to reduce subsidised grain exports during the first year of the world farm trade agreement. It used under 10 percent of its wheat and only 30 percent of its subsidised export limit for other grains.
A potential trigger for a renewed grain subsidy war would be a decision by the United States to revive the Export Enhancement Programme (EEP), which was put into mothballs early this year.
The U.S. agricultural attache in Brussels, George Pope, told the conference that Washington was watching EU export subsidies very closely but declined to give any hint of future action.
"Time will have to tell as events unfold in the market place what our reaction might be," he said.
Meanwhile the plunge in grain prices looks as if it will force the EU to reverse policy on output controls.

Roberts said there was a risk that the amount of land farmers would have to leave idle during the 1998 harvest season to qualify for EU aid payments would have to be revised upwards substantially after being cut during the past three years.
For the 1997 harvest, grain farmers had to idle five percent of their farmland under a rotational set-aside scheme.
